> @MarcoBonechi The claim that Hadith are unverifiable because they originate within the Muslim tradition confuses source origin with methodological rigor. In response to the risk of fabrication, early scholars developed ʿIlm al-Ḥadīth, a structured system of historical criticism that scrutinized every report through two independent filters: isnād, which traced each narration through a verifiable chain of transmitters whose biographies, integrity, memory, and physical possibility of contact were rigorously examined, and matn, which assessed the content itself for contradictions with the Qur’an, established facts, or stronger reports. Crucially, this system did not assume authenticity by default; it produced a formal grading hierarchyDemands for “objective verification” often apply modern scientific standards that are impossible for any ancient history; by those standards, much of what we know about figures like Alexander the Great or Socrates would also collapse, despite relying on later, partisan sources with far less source-tracking than Hadith provides. Finally, the tradition is not monolithic: internal scholarly disagreement across schools and centuries functions as peer review, reinforcing that Hadith evaluation operates as a living historical discipline, not blind faith.

> ⁠@KaoriIto-h5r 1. Spiritual Legacy  
> 	•	Muhammad revived and established strict monotheism in a region dominated by tribal polytheism.  
> 	•	He emphasized that God is One, transcendent, and beyond idols or images — a belief that today is shared by over 1.9 billion Muslims worldwide.  
> 	•	His teachings about prayer, fasting, charity, and community worship created one of the world’s most unified spiritual communities.  
>   
> ⸻  
>   
> 2. Ethical and Moral Reform  
> 	•	He taught fairness in trade, honesty in speech, kindness to orphans, and respect for parents.  
> 	•	Strongly condemned racism: “No Arab is superior to a non-Arab, and no white over black, except by piety.” This message of equality still inspires justice movements.  
> 	•	He worked to limit cycles of tribal revenge, teaching forgiveness and patience.  
>   
> ⸻  
>   
> 3. Social Justice  
> 	•	Elevated the rights of women in 7th-century Arabia: inheritance rights, the right to own property, the right to consent to marriage.  
> 	•	Banned female infanticide, which was common in pre-Islamic Arabia.  
> 	•	Improved conditions for slaves and promoted their emancipation — while the system of slavery wasn’t fully abolished in his time, he made freeing slaves a highly virtuous act.  
>   
> ⸻  
>   
> 4. Legal and Political Innovations  
> 	•	Introduced the Constitution of Medina, often considered one of the first written constitutions in history. It established principles of religious tolerance, rights for minorities (including Jews and Christians), and collective responsibility for security.  
> 	•	Laid the groundwork for systems of law (Sharia), which influenced governance across Asia, Africa, and Europe for centuries.  
>   
> ⸻  
>   
> 5. Intellectual and Scientific Spark  
> 	•	Muhammad emphasized seeking knowledge as a religious duty. This encouragement sparked the Islamic Golden Age, when Muslim scholars preserved, expanded, and passed on Greek, Persian, Indian, and Chinese knowledge.  
> 	•	Contributions in mathematics (algebra, algorithms), medicine (Avicenna), optics (Ibn al-Haytham), astronomy, and geography had direct impact on the European Renaissance.  
>   
> ⸻  
>   
> 6. Economic and Trade Development  
> 	•	His example as a fair merchant inspired ethical business practices.  
> 	•	Islam’s spread through trade routes (Arabia, Africa, Asia) created vast networks of exchange that connected civilizations, boosting global commerce and cultural exchange.  
>   
> ⸻  
>   
> 7. Unity and Civilization-Building  
> 	•	His teachings helped unify the fractured tribes of Arabia into a single community (the Ummah).  
> 	•	This unity expanded outward, giving rise to empires that became bridges between East and West.  
> 	•	Islamic architecture, art, literature, and calligraphy enriched global culture.  
>   
> ⸻  
>   
> 8. Humanitarian Values  
> 	•	Charity (zakat) became a pillar of faith — institutionalizing support for the poor, travelers, widows, and orphans.  
> 	•	Strong emphasis on community welfare — hospitals, schools, and shelters were funded through religious charity.  
> 	•	Ethical dietary rules (no usury, no alcohol, no gambling) aimed to reduce social harms.  
>   
> ⸻  
>   
> 9. Global Influence Today  
> 	•	The Quran, his central teaching, is the most widely memorized and recited book in the world.  
> 	•	His sayings (hadiths) continue to shape Muslim law, ethics, and daily life.  
> 	•	The Islamic calendar, rituals like Ramadan and Hajj, and cultural identity of Muslims are directly tied to his guidance.  
> 	•	Non-Muslim thinkers (like Thomas Carlyle, Gandhi, Lamartine) also praised his sincerity, leadership, and transformative power.  
>   
> ⸻  
>   
> ✅ In summary: Muhammad’s impact is seen in global religion, law, ethics, women’s rights, knowledge, culture, and unity. He turned a tribal, divided society into a faith-driven civilization whose influence still stretches worldwide.

I find the professor's perspectives very interesting. It provides a non-faith and non-muslim academic window to understanding how Islam may be viewed. I also like how the professor adds some depth by explaining the geopolitical landscape.

I do however think that using Sabeos's perspective to derive the key mission of Prophet Muhammad and his strategy is flawed.

Using Sebeos alone to teach Muhammad’s character, mission, and objectives is limited because his account is shaped by three factors:

1. Religious framework – As a Christian bishop, Sebeos could respect Muhammad as a lawgiver but not as a prophet, which colors his perspective.


2. Geopolitical context – Armenia was directly affected by Arab expansion, so Muhammad’s movement was inevitably framed as a political and military threat.


3. Subjective selection – Sebeos highlights themes relevant to Armenians (biblical lineage, survival between empires), not an objective account of Muhammad’s mission.



By contrast, the Qur’an itself offers the most direct window into Muhammad’s character and objectives, since it reflects his message in real time. Its core emphases are:

Monotheism and salvation.

Lessons from earlier prophets and nations.

A framework for ethical and social life.


While hadith studies add depth through preserved sayings and actions, even if their authenticity is debated, the Qur’an alone provides a more reliable, comprehensive foundation for understanding Muhammad’s mission than external, subjective narratives like Sebeos.

Dear Professor / Creator of Predictive History,
Thank you for putting the time and effort into creating this lecture series. Your presentation style is highly engaging, and your passion for tracing the macro-patterns of human civilization is evident.
However, as a student of history, I must respectfully suggest revisiting the historiography regarding pre-Islamic Arabia and the early Islamic conquests. While using comparative historical frameworks—such as mapping the French Revolution or the Taiping Rebellion onto different eras—can be a useful pedagogical tool, applying this specific modern socio-economic prism to 7th-century Arabia leads to significant anachronisms and factual discrepancies.
Here is a methodological breakdown of why this specific historical framework does not fit the rise of Islam, along with some recommended reading from leading Western scholars in the field.
1. The Methodological Flaw: Historical Reductionism
From a sociological and historical perspective, applying an 18th- or 19th-century class-struggle template (peasants vs. landlords, or bourgeoisie vs. monarchy) to Late Antiquity Arabia is an exercise in historical reductionism.
• Differing Social Topography: Pre-Islamic Arabia was not an agrarian feudal society with "landlords" hoarding wealth from "landless peasants." It was a pastoral-nomadic and mercantile society.
• Kinship over Class: Power and social survival were dictated by complex tribal affiliations, clan protection, and bloodlines—what the famous historian Ibn Khaldun termed 'asabiyyah (social cohesion/tribal solidarity). When Muhammad was persecuted in Mecca, it was not a class war; it was a profound disruption of the existing tribal and economic hierarchy centered around the Kaaba's idol trade.
• The Danger of a Single Prism: Attempting to force every historical event into a Western, post-Enlightenment revolutionary framework ignores the unique socio-cultural realities of the Middle East. It inadvertently strips the Arabs, Persians, and Byzantines of their actual historical context.
2. The Reality of the Conquests
The lecture suggests the Arab conquests succeeded primarily due to a "revolutionary zeal" against empires. While ideological unity was undoubtedly the catalyst that pointed the warring Arab tribes outward (much like Genghis Khan uniting the steppe nomads), the geopolitical reality is more structural. The Byzantine and Sassanid Persian empires did not fall to the Arabs because they were overthrown by peasant revolutions; they collapsed because they had just fought a catastrophic, 26-year-long war of annihilation with each other (602–628 CE). The Arab armies emerged into a power vacuum against two completely bankrupt, militarily exhausted states.
3. Recommended Reading from Western Scholars
To help bridge this gap, I highly recommend stepping away from fringe revisionist theories (like those relying heavily on Sebeos to frame Islam as a purely Jewish-Arab reconquest) and looking into the modern consensus of Late Antiquity scholars. Here are a few foundational texts by respected Western academics:
• Fred M. Donner – Muhammad and the Believers: At the Origins of Islam
• Donner (Professor of Near Eastern History at UChicago) brilliantly reconstructs the early years of the Islamic movement, contextualizing it within the religious environment of Late Antiquity without relying on modern political frameworks.
• Hugh Kennedy – The Great Arab Conquests: How the Spread of Islam Changed the World We Live In
• Kennedy provides a masterful, grounded military and political history of how the Arab armies actually defeated the Romans and Persians, focusing on logistics, tribal dynamics, and imperial exhaustion rather than Marxist revolution.
• Marshall G. S. Hodgson – The Venture of Islam (Volume 1)
• A monumental work that specifically warns against using Eurocentric frameworks to judge Islamic history, offering a much more accurate structural analysis of the era.
• Robert Hoyland – In God's Path: The Arab Conquests and the Creation of an Islamic Empire
• Hoyland does an excellent job of incorporating non-Muslim contemporary sources to build a realistic picture of the conquests, avoiding the pitfalls of extreme revisionism.
Thank you again for the thought-provoking content. I hope you will take these constructive critiques and sources in the academic spirit they are intended, as incorporating them will only make your comparative history series stronger and more historically sound

> The claim that the Sunnah was not written down until 100 or 200 years later is historically inaccurate and overlooks the nature of Islamic documentation, which was characterized by a unique scientific rigor. Here are the facts:

> Transmission was not purely oral; rather, there were what we call 'Sahifas' (written scrolls).

> 2. The Science of Men and Isnad (The Science of Bio-Bibliography):  
> Islam is the only religion that invented 'Ilm al-Jarh wa al-Ta’dil' (The Science of Validation and Criticism). > * If a narrator lied even once in their life (even in worldly matters), their narration is rejected forever.  
> * This system is the most precise historical documentation system known to humanity, known as 'Isnad Verification' (Chain of narration verification).   
> 3. Responding to 'Follower Bias' (Neutral POV):  
> Hadith science did not rely on 'emotion'; it relied on Cross-referencing.   
> * Hadith scholars compared the narrations of thousands of students from a single teacher; if one of them made a mistake, the others exposed him.  
> * The Sahaba (Companions) and Tabi’un (Successors) were not a single political front; they had major political disagreements. Despite this, they did not change the 'texts' of the Hadiths to serve their interests. If there were forgery, we would see blatant contradictions between the narrations of opposing sides, yet we find agreement in the core of legislation and biography.   
> 4. Memorization as a Supporting Tool:  
> Arabs at that time possessed exceptional memorization skills (due to the oral nature of their language). Relying on the 'heart' (memory) was not a 'Telephone game' as some imagine; it was a disciplined memorization backed by written documentation for review.   
>   
> Here to sum things up   
> The time gap you mentioned(100-200 years) is the gap of 'Official Comprehensive Codification' (bound books), not a gap of 'Documentation and Writing.' Modern science today, through discovered manuscripts, has proven that the Sunnah was documented since the first century.

Professor, I found your comment about how we know less about Muhammad (peace be upon him) interesting.
It’s true that his sayings weren’t written down immediately, but what’s remarkable is that Muslims developed one of the earliest and strictest verification systems in history — the isnād, or chain of narration.
Each report about him was preserved with a full list of transmitters, and scholars examined every person’s reliability, memory, and life dates before accepting it.

In a sense, it’s like historical peer review — centuries before modern historiography.
That’s why for Muslims, the authentic hadith collections aren’t random oral memories but carefully cross-checked records.

You might find it interesting how much internal criticism existed in this field — most reports were actually rejected.
It shows that early Muslim scholars understood the danger of misinformation and built a system specifically to prevent it.

> ​@melissakmz23Hi, thanks for the discussion. I looked into the verses you mentioned (41:9–12 and 79:27–30), and I realized that what looks like a contradiction actually comes from how we assume the Arabic word thumma works.  
>   
> In Classical Arabic, thumma does not always mean “then” in a strict chronological sense. It also regularly means:  
>   
> “moreover,”  
>   
> “in addition,”  
>   
> “furthermore,”  
>   
> or a shift in topic rather than a sequence in time.  
>   
> This isn’t an interpretation I’m inventing — it’s how the word is used throughout the Qur’an itself.  
>   
> Two very clear examples:  
>   
> 1. Surah al-Baqarah 2:29  
>   
> The verse says God created the earth and thumma “turned to the heaven.”  
> But other verses show the heavens existed first, so classical scholars all agree that thumma here means “moreover”, not a literal “afterward.”  
>   
> 2. Surah 3:111  
>   
> Here thumma is used in a purely rhetorical way to add emphasis, not as a time sequence.  
>   
> Since the Qur’an itself uses thumma in both temporal and non-temporal ways, we can’t assume that every instance means “next in time.”  
>   
> So when one set of verses mentions the earth first and another mentions the sky first, the difference does not automatically indicate acontradiction — it can simply be a shift in emphasis or focus, not a timeline. This is completely normal in classical Arabic style.  
>   
> In that light, the passages aren’t actually contradicting each other; the apparent conflict comes from assuming a single rigid meaning of thumma, which the Qur’an’s own usage doesn’t support.  
>   
> I just wanted to share this because it helped clarify the issue for me. Hope it’s useful, and I appreciate the conversation.

Thank you Mr. Jiang 
I may have misunderstood your point, but I felt like you suggested that Prophet Muhammad was responsible for the military expansions into the Sassanian Empire, parts of Byzantium, and other regions to spread Islam.
However, when we look at both the Quran and historical timelines, this seems very unlikely. The Quran repeatedly emphasizes that faith cannot be forced ("There is no compulsion in religion", Quran 2:256) and that the Prophet's role was only to deliver the message, not to compel belief or expand territory.
Additionally, from a historical perspective, the major conquests of the Sassanian Empire and large parts of Byzantium took place after Prophet Muhammad’s death in 632 CE, during the period of the early caliphates. This makes it difficult to attribute those expansions directly to him.
So based on both the Quranic message and historical evidence, it seems more accurate to distinguish between the Prophet’s mission and the later political expansions carried out after his lifetime.
I say this respectfully, and I'm open to learning if there are sources that suggest otherwise.

(1:28) If what we know about any person is through the literature we find within their culture, then I would argue that the prophet of Islam has a plethora of details written about his life available to us through his biographies and sayings. Quite a lot more than many other influential figures in history.  These include:
1. The "Seerah", or biography by Ibn Hisham 
2. The "Hadith" or "sayings" which can be found compiled in the collection of Al-Bukhari, Muslim, Ahmad bin Hanbal, Ibn Majah, Al-Muwataa, and several others.
3. Other external sources.
(2:29) The monotheism was essentially shared amongst the descendants of Abraham, though the Israelites had more prophets than any other descendants according to the Bible. Nonetheless,  the Bible does mention that Israelites (descendants of Isaac son of Abraham) also experienced idol worship with Moses and later during the life of Elijah by worshiping "Baal" and "Moloch"  and engaging in child sacrifice to such idols. Islamic sources on the other hand mention that although many or most Arabs (descendants of Ishmael son of Abraham) had engaged in idolatry by the time Islam began to appear, there still remained a very small minority that held onto Abrahamic monotheism but had no prophets or scriptures like the Israelites had. What ever Abraham had received was mostly lost amongst his Arab descendants except for the ritual of the annual pilgrimage to the house in Mecca. Yet, even that ritual became tainted with idolatry through the centuries between the time of Abrahamand Ishmael,  and the time of Muhammad. 
This minority  of monotheists eventually formed the first theologically coherent group in Mecca and were subjected to persecution as a result, because they challenged the polytheistic belief system by attempting to revive monotheism. That included boycotting, ridicule  and eventually torture especiallyof the slaves. That persecution lasted 13 years before the migration to what is now known as Medinah.
(4:13) Quite true, there are many parallels between the Moses and Muhammad historically.
(13:59) The Arab nomad community in 7th century Arabia was an "oral culture" they were highly skilled in poetry and because few knew how to write ✍️ they depended heavily on memorization.
(39:33) The only missing element in this argument I would say are
i. Intimidation of existing powers towards emerging powers
ii. The existence of power vacuums that need to be filled. 
These are (non-religious) factors that have existed throughout human history that have shaped borders and empires.
(39:43) We have to be careful here with terminology because Muhammad identied himself as "the last prophet", he did not identify himself as "Messiah". The expression "Messiah" is reserved in the Quran for Jesus the son of Mary, whom Muslims like Christians believe will return at some time in the future. The Jewish community  await their own Messiah.
(43:10) One of the most overlooked characteristics that made Islam appealing to other nations was the abolishing of usury and debt compounding effect which literally in the past empoverished the common folks and resulted in their financial enslaving to the landlords and elites. The only permitted transactional currency was gold and silver which helped retain the value of money for centuries.
(44:47) There is an important overlooked aspect here. That is monotheism in the pagan Arab environment was seen as a "disruptive" idea 💡.  Disruptive to established hierarchies, businesses and financial dealing. Before Islam, prostitution was a business,  gambling was a business,  alcohol was a business,  selling idols was a business,  selling weapons to fighting tribes was a business. Selling slaves was a business. Usury was a big business.  Creating a coherent society with Laws giving equal rights "threatened" all these businesses and threatened the pagan Arab elites.
Monotheism triumphed in Arabia eventually because Arabia was not an established empire like Rome and Persia. As noted earlier Rome made stamping out monotheism a prime target that was difficult to tame. This could not happen in Arabia because Arabia was a tribal environment and even though most Arabs were pagan , they still remembered the monotheistic legacy of their father Abraham, which gradually gathered a foothold.

Analyzing this video from Predictive History is highly interesting because it employs a sociopolitical approach and historical analogies (such as the French Revolution or the Taiping Rebellion) to explain the early success of Islam.
The professor strongly emphasizes the aspect of “Economic and Social Revolution” as the primary driving force.

However, if we aim to offer constructive academic criticism and enrich the literature he uses, there are several crucial points that could be added to make his perspective more balanced:

1. Deepening “Internal” Literature (Sirah Nabawiyyah)

The professor claims that “we do not know much about Muhammad” and that “the Qur’an barely mentions him.” This is a point that can be critically addressed.

Input: Although the Qur’an is theocentric (God-centered), the literature of Sirah Nabawiyyah (the Prophet’s biography), such as the works of Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Hisham, is highly detailed.
The critique here is that the professor relies too heavily on external sources (such as the writings of the Christian bishop Sebeos) and overlooks the highly rigorous Arab oral tradition (the sciences of Hadith and Rijal).

Suggested Literature: Incorporate the methodology of Mustafa Azami in Studies in Early Hadith Literature to demonstrate that the Arab oral tradition possessed a far more sophisticated verification system than mere “folklore transmission.”


2. Spiritual Dimension vs. Historical Materialism

The professor tends to interpret the movement of Prophet Muhammad through the lens of Historical Materialism—that its primary motivations were land, debt abolition, and resistance against landlords.

Input: This risks reducing a religious movement to merely a peasant revolt. If it were purely driven by economic factors, the movement would likely have collapsed after the Prophet’s death (as many revolutions have). The loyalty of the companions, especially during events such as the Conquest of Mecca, indicates a profound transformation of character and spirituality, not merely incentives like war booty or land.

Suggested Literature: Refer to Martin Lings’ Muhammad: His Life Based on the Earliest Sources to better understand the contemplative dimension and spiritual charisma that cannot be explained solely through sociopolitical revolution theory.


3. The Concept of the “Promised Land”

The professor states that Prophet Muhammad promised a “Promised Land” from the Nile to the Tigris to his followers.

Input: Theologically and historically, the concept of a “Promised Land” in Islam is not identical to the Zionist concept in Judaism. The primary focus of early Islamic expansion was often futuhat (openings) to facilitate da‘wah (the spread of the message), rather than territorial occupation based on ethnic entitlement. The term jihad in early literature is more closely associated with ensuring religious freedom than with reclaiming land.

4. Balancing the “Whitewashing” Theory of History

The professor theorizes that the history of Muhammad was “whitewashed” by later empires to prevent people from rebelling.

Input: While this theory is intriguing, it should be balanced with the fact that classical Islamic literature is remarkably transparent in documenting internal conflicts (such as the Battles of Jamal and Siffin). If there had been a total effort to sanitize history, such painful conflicts among the companions would likely have been erased.

Suggested Literature: Refer to Fred Donner’s works, such as The Early Islamic Conquests or Muhammad and the Believers. Donner offers a more nuanced perspective, portraying the early movement as a “Community of Believers” (mu’minun)—inclusive, yet firmly rooted in a consistent revelation.


---

Conclusion (Feedback for the Professor)

The revolutionary analogies he employs are helpful for modern audiences to grasp the scale of transformation brought by Prophet Muhammad. However, to achieve greater academic accuracy, he should:

Avoid underestimating the richness and detail of Hadith and Sirah traditions.

Incorporate the dimension of moral and individual transformation as the foundation of the social revolution.

Distinguish clearly between “political expansion” and the “prophetic mission,” so that it is not reduced to a purely material conquest movement.

### **@OmarElghamry1**
[View on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C9rzPGJ0wm4&lc=Ugx2qE9POh1YXBJ2_2F4AaABAg)

The Arabs were uniquely skilled in language, especially in composing rhymed and highly sophisticated poetry (الشعر). This was their strongest cultural domain, and words held immense value in their society. One clear example is Souq Okaz, where poets would gather to recite and even “compete” with their verses. Poetry was not just expression—it was a form of prestige, influence, and cultural identity, and in many ways, words themselves were “traded” and celebrated at the highest level. This makes the Arabs arguably the first society to elevate and institutionalize poetic expression in such a public and competitive way.

When they first heard the Qur’an, they immediately recognized that its linguistic structure and style were extraordinarily difficult to replicate. This is significant because the Qur’an itself challenged them—despite their mastery of language—to produce anything like it. Yet, they were unable to do so, and that challenge remains unmet to this day.

You have read and quoted from the Bible, so it raises a fair question: why not examine the Qur’an with the same attention?

Additionally, how could Muhammad challenge the Jews regarding their own scriptures and stories—matters that were typically known only to their scholars? Earlier, you suggested that groups like the Ebionites migrated to Arabia and later influenced Islam. However, an alternative explanation is that some of these groups came to the Arab world because their own texts mentioned the coming of a prophet appearing in that region, referred to as “Muhammad” or “Ahmad.” They may have expected this prophet to emerge from among themselves, but were surprised when he came from the Arabs, which contributed to their rejection.

Moreover, the Prophet recited passages of the Qur’an directly to them, recounting narratives consistent with their traditions. If the position is uncertainty about how this knowledge was acquired, that is understandable. However, attributing it solely to trade interactions does not sufficiently explain the depth and specificity of the information presented.

Continuing the fact-check (Claude AI, strict non-Islamic sources only) — Part 2 of 2:
[11:49] The Arab conquests are not "one of the greatest unsolved mysteries in world history." Mainstream historians have studied this extensively. By 628 CE both the Byzantine and Sassanid empires had exhausted their resources after a catastrophic 30-year war. The Sassanid Empire then cycled through 12 rulers in 14 years. Trade routes had been ruined. The Arabian Peninsula had meanwhile been unified under a single leadership for the first time. This is well-established scholarly consensus, not an open mystery.
[33:17] The Justinian plague death toll is significantly understated. Scholarly estimates range from 25 to 100 million deaths, with some placing the mortality rate at a quarter to half the entire Mediterranean population. More importantly, the instructor omits a detail that directly supports his own argument: nomadic Arab tribes largely escaped the plague because they moved through desert and semi-desert regions. The plague is actually part of the explanation for Arab military success — and the instructor oddly leaves it out while discussing both topics simultaneously.
[17:00] Canudos is in the state of Bahia in northeastern Brazil, not Europe. The instructor catches himself, but the slip is notable in a world history course.
[22:19] Describing the Arabian Peninsula as "the most Cosmopolitan center in the world" in 600 CE is not supportable. Constantinople had an estimated population of 300,000 to 500,000 people. Alexandria, Ctesiphon, and Chang'an were all far larger and more diverse than Mecca. Mecca was a significant trading town — not a world metropolis.
[44:41] The instructor claims the monotheism-vs-polytheism framing was invented later to disguise Islam's revolutionary origins. But the Sebeos passage he himself quoted — the earliest non-Islamic source he cites — explicitly describes Muhammad telling Arabs they had "abandoned their vain cults" and calling them back to Abrahamic monotheism. The conflict appears in the primary sources from the very beginning. His own evidence directly contradicts his conclusion.
Overall: The core thesis about exhausted empires and socially receptive populations has genuine mainstream support. But accumulated errors on river names, plague figures, the illiteracy claim, Quranic content, and basic geography mean a student relying on this lecture alone would walk away with a noticeably distorted picture of the record.

### **@geosenseagroproject987**
[View on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C9rzPGJ0wm4&lc=UgyXioU4cyQnu7deEpl4AaABAg)

I like to criticise some points made by Prof Jiang with help of gemini proof read:

The lecture seem over-politicizing Islam

He treats Islam like it was mainly a political program to:
unite tribes,
overthrow empires,
redistribute land,
cancel debt,
end persecution.

That framing misses the timeline and the “center of gravity” of early Islam:

Meccan period (about 13 years): Muslims had no state, no army, no conquest agenda. The core message was tawhid (God’s oneness), accountability, afterlife, moral reform, and rejecting idolatry. If Muhammad’s main goal was political revolution, Mecca is a strange strategy: it was mostly preaching, patience, persecution, and survival.

Medinan period: governance and warfare appear, but largely as responses to real security threats and state-building needs after migration.
So his story reads history backwards: he starts with later political outcomes (empire, conquest) and projects them as Muhammad’s original “primary intent.”

A more accurate frame is: theology → community → law → state, not “revolution → religion as tool.”

Underestimating theological depth

He portrays Islam as basically:
“Return Arabs to Yahweh / Bible monotheism; then use that to build a revolutionary movement.”
But Islam’s theological core isn’t just “Biblical content” with Arabic packaging. It’s distinct in major ways:

Tawhid is not only “one God,” but a full worldview: no intermediaries with divine authority, no divine incarnation, no tribal chosenness, no inherited guilt, no salvation via someone else’s sacrifice.

Revelation as Qur’an is not “Muhammad retelling Bible stories.” It’s presented as direct, structured revelation, with a different literary form and theological goals (guidance, moral transformation, law).

Prophethood in Islam is not “messiah politics.” A prophet is primarily a messenger calling to God and reform of worship and ethics.

His lecture also downplays what actually motivates people long-term in Islamic sources:
fear of accountability,
love of God,
hope in mercy,
moral discipline,
community worship.

He replaces those with “revolutionary zeal,” which is only one possible lens and often not the main one.

Misrepresenting sources
He makes several source claims that are misleading.

1) “We don’t know much about Muhammad; we know more about Jesus.”
Historically, we have a large corpus about Muhammad’s life compared to most ancient figures:
Qur’an (not biography, but early primary text tied to the Prophet’s mission)
Hadith literature with isnād methodology (chains of transmission)

Sīrah (biography) traditions
early documents and treaties cited in Islamic historiography
You can debate details and reliability of specific reports (scholars do), but saying “we don’t know much” is exaggerated.

2) “Qur’an doesn’t really mention him.”
The Qur’an doesn’t mention many prophets by name frequently in a biographical way. It addresses Muhammad constantly as “Messenger/Prophet.” Not being “biographical” isn’t the same as “not mentioning him.”

3) “Earliest document is a Christian bishop 20–30 years after 632.”
Non-Muslim references exist early, yes, but implying that Muslim tradition is basically later propaganda is too sweeping. Early Islamic memory and writing began early, even if later compiled more systematically.

4) His use of that bishop quote
Even if a non-Muslim source says certain things, it doesn’t automatically prove Muhammad’s aims were “land conquest for Abraham’s sons.” It proves what that observer thought or heard—possibly through rumor, polemics, or limited understanding.

So he treats a fragmentary outsider text as a decisive “key” and then builds a whole narrative on it.
Ethnicizing Abrahamic covenant
This is a major conceptual distortion.
He argues something like:
Abraham covenant = land from Nile to Tigris
Arabs are Abraham’s children through Ishmael
therefore Arabs are promised the land
therefore jihad is reclaiming Abrahamic land rights
That’s not Islamic doctrine.

Key Islamic points:
Islam rejects ethnic spiritual superiority: no “chosen race”.
Qur’an’s emphasis is faith and righteousness, not bloodline.
Even Abraham’s status in Islam is primarily about submission to God, not land entitlement.
Early Islam rapidly became multi-ethnic; it did not behave like an “Arab ethnic reclamation” ideology.

Also, his covenant mapping is shaky even within the Bible tradition because “promised land” interpretations vary widely among Jewish and Christian theologies. He presents one maximalist land reading as if it is the only reading, then assigns it to Islam.

A better way to say it:

Islam connects to Abraham as a model of monotheism and surrender to God.

It does not teach “Arabs inherit Abraham’s real estate.”

### **@Halartalpur**
[View on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C9rzPGJ0wm4&lc=UgyjIz1dniGWuYRGmU94AaABAg)

🔍 Let’s go into full detail and end this confusion once and for all…

⚠ Disclaimer: People often misinterpret age. Even today, it’s hard to guess someone’s real age based only on facial or body features. There are many people who look far younger than they are — for example, Andrew Garfield, the Spider-Man 🕷 actor, is 42 years old! Hard to believe, right? 😅

🧮 Let’s do some simple calculations:

🕋 Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) was around 53 years old at the time of the consummation of marriage.
He received Prophethood at 40 years of age.

Now, Aisha (RA) was among the first 20 people to accept Islam — meaning she had to be old enough to repeat words and understand basic speech.

Even if we go with an extreme assumption — let’s say she was just 1 year old at that time (which is obviously an exaggerated and flawed argument, but let’s go with it for the sake of logic) — then:

👉 53 - 40 = 13 years
👉 13 + 1 (her minimum possible age) = 14 years old at the time of marriage
👉 She moved in after 3 years → 14 + 3 = 17 years old

🧠 This deliberately “wrong” argument should make it clear that the common misconception doesn’t hold up under even basic reasoning.

🧩 Let’s try a more realistic approach:

🔎 A quick Google search shows:

Abu Bakr (RA) accepted Islam shortly after the Prophet (ﷺ) began receiving revelations — likely within the first year.

He’s regarded as the first adult male outside the Prophet’s family to embrace Islam.

Aisha (RA), his daughter, accepted Islam in the very early days — possibly being the 18th or 19th person to do so.

So, the earlier assumption of her being 1 year old is clearly wrong ❌.

📜 Early Conversion Facts:

🕊 Aisha (RA), along with her family, accepted Islam when the Prophet’s (ﷺ) message was still private.
📅 She was likely between 6 and 10 years old at that time — old enough to understand and accept faith.

Historical records and scholarly research place her birth around 605 CE.
This means she would have been 6–10 years old when Islam began to spread privately.

🧮 Recalculation (More Reasonable Logic):

If Aisha (RA) was 6 years old when she accepted Islam,
then at the time of the consummation:

👉 53 - 40 = 13
👉 13 + 6 = 19 years old at marriage
👉 Moved after 3 years → 19 + 3 = 22 years old

💡 Final Thought:

📚 Historical context and multiple scholarly analyses suggest that Aisha (RA) was a young woman, not a child, at the time of her marriage to the Prophet (ﷺ).
It’s important to rely on context, logic, and credible historical evidence — not hearsay or misinterpretations. 🕊

Continuing the fact-check (Claude AI, strict non-Islamic sources only) — Part 1 of 2:
[4:04] Moses is correctly identified as the most mentioned figure in the Quran at 136 times — but this directly contradicts the earlier claim that "the Quran doesn't really mention Muhammad," since the Quran's focus was never on Muhammad to begin with. Internal contradiction worth noting.
[4:46] Two separate errors. Genesis 15:18 specifies the Euphrates, not the Tigris — these are different rivers in different parts of Iraq. Most biblical scholars also note that "the river of Egypt" likely refers to the Wadi el-Arish in Sinai, not the Nile. Calling the territory "basically the entire Middle East" stretches the actual text considerably.
[5:04] The Hagar story in Genesis is far messier than presented. Hagar is described as an Egyptian slave-girl. Conflict between her and Sarah was severe enough that Abraham sent Hagar away twice. The instructor presents it as a clean, sympathetic arrangement — the biblical account is far more morally fraught.
[5:48] Ishmael as father of the Arabs is a religious tradition, not established historical fact. "Ishmaelite" references in the historical record cease around the 10th century BCE while "Arab" references only begin in the 8th century BCE — a significant chronological gap. Arabic as a language also predates the timeframe in which Ishmael would have lived.
[5:56] "The Israelites eventually became the Christians" flattens centuries of complex history. The vast majority of Jewish people did not become Christians. Judaism and Christianity developed as entirely distinct traditions. Both Jewish and Christian scholars would contest this framing.
[8:56] The "illiterate merchant" claim is actively debated in modern scholarship. The Quranic word "ummi" is now understood by most academics to mean "gentile" or "one without prior scripture," not simply unable to read. Historian Juan Cole has noted that long-distance merchants trading between Arabia, Syria, and Egypt almost certainly had basic literacy. The lecture presents a contested theological interpretation as plain historical fact.
[9:33] The first revelation was around 610 CE and the Hijra was 622 CE. That is 12 years in Mecca, not 13 — a small but notable error in a lecture claiming to correct the historical record.

Historical Chronology of Evidence
The First Recorded Mention of "Arabs" (853 BC):
The earliest known mention of the "Arabs" as a distinct group comes from Assyrian Cuneiform records. Specifically, the Monolith Inscription of the Assyrian King Shalmaneser III describes a battle against a coalition of kings, one of whom was "Gindibu the Arab," who contributed 1,000 camels to the fight.

The Qedarite (Kedar) Confederation (7th Century BC):
Extensive Assyrian and Babylonian administrative records confirm the existence of the "Qedarites" (Kedar), a powerful North Arabian tribal confederation. These records match the period and location of the group identified in genealogical traditions as the descendants of Ishmael, providing a historical anchor for that lineage long before Islamic records.

The Ancestor Adnan in Early Epigraphy:
While the name Adnan is central to Muhammad's lineage, his name appears in various Pre-Islamic Safaitic and Thamudic inscriptions across the Arabian desert. These inscriptions prove that "Adnan" was a known historical or legendary figure among Northern Arabian tribes centuries before the 7th century, though these stone records do not explicitly detail his family tree back to Abraham.

The Emergence of the Quraysh (5th–7th Century AD):
The specific tribe of the Prophet, the Quraysh, begins to appear in regional records as a dominant commercial and political force in the 5th century. External Byzantine and Syriac chronicles from the early 7th century (dated around 634 AD) mention the "Arabs of Muhammad" immediately following the initial conquests, confirming the family's established leadership and their role in the unification of the Hijaz tribes.

This is misleading. The Qur’an names Muhammad ﷺ and commands believers to follow his example and guidance (33:21; 59:7). 
Beyond that, Muslims preserved an enormous, rigorously-sourced corpus about his life: the two most authentic ḥadīth collections alone contain ~7,500 reports each (with repetitions), selected with strict chain-of-transmission (isnād) criteria. 
Whole books detail his person and daily habits (e.g., al-Tirmidhī’s Shamāʾil), including physical description, worship, leadership, and family life. 
His teachings cover marital ethics down to practical etiquette—“The best of you are those best to their wives”—and even step-by-step guidance for post-intimacy purification (ghusl). 
Classical biographies and narrator dictionaries (sīra and rijāl) span dozens of volumes, documenting thousands of individuals linked to him and to the transmission of his sayings. 

Far from being unknown, the Prophet’s is arguably  the most thoroughly documented lives in pre-modern history, and his Sunnah explains the Qur’an and grounds Islamic law.

The problem with the Sunni belief that Abu Bakr was the caliph (successor) is that humans are corruptible, and only Allah knows what is in the hearts of people. Abu Bakr, according to Sunni belief, was the closest companion of the Prophet and was selected by a group of people. However, Shias believe it does not work that way. Allah would not leave His religion—sent with truth—to be decided by people as to who represents Islam.
In fact, Umar and Uthman were also chosen differently—some through selection, others through a council. Imam Ali, according to Sunnis, became the fourth caliph by default. All four were chosen using different methods and criteria, which does not make sense.
That is why the Shia position is the only logical one: the Prophet absolutely appointed a successor—Imam Ali (عليه السلام). Look at the event of Ghadir Khumm. It is the clearest evidence. The Prophet left behind the Qur’an and his Ahl al-Bayt (his holy household and progeny), and said that as long as you follow both, you will not be misguided.
Alhamdulillah, the Shias have followed the correct path of the twelve infallible, divinely appointed successors after the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), starting with Imam Ali (عليه السلام), followed by Imam Hasan and Imam Husayn (عليهم السلام), his grandsons who sacrificed their lives to preserve Islam from the corruption of Muawiya and Yazid.
This is why divine appointment is a necessity for preserving Islam and the true teachings of the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). Shias uphold this truth, and it can be seen even in modern times. Shias in Iran, Lebanon, Yemen, and Iraq are among those actively resisting oppression and supporting the Palestinians, while many Sunni governments—such as Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Turkey—have taken different political positions.

Unlike earlier scriptures, which were subject to later human alteration, the Qur’an remains preserved word-for-word in its original Arabic as the direct speech of God.
It is also important to understand the distinction between a prophet (Nabī) and a messenger (Rasūl). While all messengers are prophets, not all prophets are messengers. Messengers—such as Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad—were sent with divine scripture to resolve disputes among people and establish clear guidance.
Historically, the downfall of major empires such as the Persian and Roman empires is viewed, in this theological framework, as a consequence of rejecting divine guidance. ### **@abinurzhan**
[View on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C9rzPGJ0wm4&lc=UgzpzwQ2Clh1Wjm1eCx4AaABAg)

The video contains minor facts and major discrepancies. The speaker attempts to force 7th-century tribal history into a modern Marxist "class struggle" template, which leads to glaring historical contradictions.
Here are the major flaws in his lecture:
 * The Tolerance Paradox: The speaker claims pre-Islamic Arabia was an incredibly open-minded "utopia of religious tolerance." If they were so perfectly tolerant of new ideas, why did the Quraysh violently persecute, boycott, and exile Muhammad and his early followers for 13 years just for preaching monotheism?
 * Inventing "Landlords": He frames the rise of Islam as a peasant revolution against "landlords." Pre-Islamic Arabia was a deeply tribal, pastoral, and mercantile society. It was not a feudal, agrarian society. Applying 18th-century European revolutionary concepts here is completely anachronistic.
 * Geopolitical Reality: The claim that Arabia was the "most advanced and cosmopolitan center in the world" is historically false. The Byzantine and Sassanid empires ignored the deep Arabian Peninsula because it lacked rivers and major agricultural wealth. They viewed the Arabs much like the sedentary Chinese empires viewed the Mongols—as divided, harsh-environment nomads to be managed as buffer states, not as a peer threat to be conquered.
 * Why the Empires Actually Fell: The Arab conquests succeeded rapidly not because of advanced Arabian technological superiority, but primarily because the Byzantines and Sassanids were entirely bankrupt and militarily exhausted from a devastating, 26-year-long war with each other.
The speaker is trying to cram complex Late Antiquity history into a pre-packaged narrative about global revolutions, completely missing the actual socio-economic realities of the time.

### **@bishnie**
[View on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C9rzPGJ0wm4&lc=UgxNgdb2QhTyAuZzhtZ4AaABAg)

[0:06] — "We know very little about Muhammad — less than we know about Jesus"



Actually backwards. A Syriac chronicle from around 640 CE — just 8 years after Muhammad's death — already mentions "the Arabs of Muhammad" fighting Rome. A Byzantine Greek text from 634 CE, literally two years after his death, names him directly. Compare that to Jesus, where the earliest non-Christian mention (Tacitus) comes roughly 80 years after the crucifixion. Muhammad has earlier external confirmation relative to his death date than Jesus does. The opening premise of the entire lecture is inverted.



[1:44] — "Muhammad just means blessed one in Arabic"



Wrong. The name comes from the Arabic root Ḥ-M-D meaning "to praise," making Muhammad mean "praised" or "praiseworthy." Completely different word from "blessed." A small but basic factual error.



[1:44] — "We don't even know what his real name is"



We do. Both Muslim and non-Muslim 7th century sources, independently of each other, consistently refer to him by this name or close transliterations like "Mahmet." No serious historian treats "Muhammad" as a mysterious later title rather than his actual given name.



[1:02] — "The Quran doesn't really mention Muhammad"



Hard to understand how this made it into a lecture. His name appears explicitly four times in the Quran, an entire chapter (Surah 47) is named directly after him, and he's addressed personally throughout dozens of verses. Verifiable in 30 seconds.



[1:02] — "The Quran is in theory written by him"



Even from a purely secular-historical standpoint this misrepresents the record. Every source we have — Muslim and non-Muslim — describes Muhammad as the recipient of revelations, not their author. His companions wrote them down during his lifetime, Abu Bakr later ordered their collection, and Uthman standardized them. Framing it as "written by him" reflects neither the theological position nor the historical account.



[4:46] — "The promised land goes from the Nile to the Tigers (Tigris) in modern day Iraq — basically the entire Middle East"



Two issues here. First, the biblical text in Genesis 15:18 actually says "from the river of Egypt to the great river, the Euphrates" — not the Tigris. Second, and more importantly, most biblical scholars note that "the river of Egypt" most likely refers to the Wadi el-Arish, a small stream in the Sinai, not the Nile itself. The instructor casually expands this covenant to cover "the entire Middle East" which goes well beyond what the text actually says. The promised land in Genesis is the land of Canaan and surrounding regions — significant, but not "the entire Middle East."



[5:41] — "Ishmael went to the Arabian Desert and he is the father of the Arab people"



This is far more complicated than the instructor presents. It is a widely held religious tradition shared by Islam, some Jewish sources (starting with Josephus in the 1st century CE), and many Christians — but it is not straightforward historical fact. Secular scholars at the Middle East Forum and Oxford have pointed out that references to "Ishmaelites" as a people group cease in records by around the 10th century BCE, while references to "Arabs" only begin in the mid-8th century BCE, leaving a significant gap. The linguistic evidence also doesn't neatly support it — Arabic as a language predates the timeframe in which Ishmael would have lived. The claim that all Arabs descend from Ishmael is a religious tradition, not an established historical fact, and presenting it as settled history in an academic lecture is misleading.



[6:30] — The Hadith described as just "oral stories passed down generation to generation"



This dramatically undersells one of the most sophisticated source-criticism methodologies in the pre-modern world. Islamic scholars developed rigorous chains of transmission (isnad), cross-referenced narrator reliability, and classified traditions into categories of soundness (sahih, hasan, da'if). Scholars like al-Bukhari applied methods that historians genuinely respect and that anticipate modern historical criticism. Calling it casual oral folklore isn't accurate.



[8:56] — "Muhammad was an illiterate merchant who had no exposure to the Bible — this proves it was a miracle"



The "illiterate" claim is actually actively debated by modern scholars. University of Michigan historian Juan Cole, a leading non-Muslim scholar of Islam, has stated that long-distance merchants of this era were always literate, and that Muhammad regularly traded up to Damascus and Gaza in the Eastern Roman Empire. The Arabic word used in the Quran — "ummi" — is now understood by most modern academic scholars to mean "gentile" or "one without a prior scripture," not "illiterate" in the simple sense. Mehdy Shaddel summarized the scholarly consensus as being "virtually unanimous" that ummi does not straightforwardly mean illiterate. The lecture presents a theologically motivated interpretation as a straightforward historical fact.



[9:33] — "He spent 13 years in Mecca preaching before the Hijra"



The traditional account places his first revelation around 610 CE and the Hijra in 622 CE. That is 12 years, not 13. Minor, but worth noting in a lecture that claims to be fixing historical inaccuracies.



[10:25] — The Constitution of Medina "promises freedom of religious expression to all people"



The instructor gets the broad point right — the Constitution of Medina is genuinely historically significant and did establish remarkable protections for the time. Both Muslim and non-Muslim scholars, including W. Montgomery Watt and Robert Serjeant, consider it an authentic early document. It did grant Jews the right to their own religion and law. However, calling it a blanket guarantee of religious freedom for everyone is an oversimplification. The document is primarily a military and political treaty between tribes, and scholars debate what it actually guaranteed and to whom. The instructor presents a modern liberal reading of a complex 7th-century document.



[11:31] — "The Muslims defeated both Empires" presented almost as miraculous without adequate explanation



The instructor then tries to solve this "mystery" with his revolutionary theory — but mainstream historians have actually already explained it quite thoroughly without needing to frame Islam as a global revolution. The Byzantine and Persian powers were unusually weak at this time, as a consequence of a catastrophic thirty-year war between the two that had depleted their manpower, resources, and morale. By contrast, the Arabian Peninsula had been united under a singular leadership for the first time. This is the mainstream scholarly explanation. The "mystery" the instructor presents as unsolved has been extensively studied and fairly well understood. Years of Sassanid-Byzantine wars had ruined trade routes and industry, and the existing Sassanid administrative structure proved inadequate when faced with the combined demands of a suddenly expanded empire. The "mystery" framing is dramatically overstated.



[17:00] — "War of the Canudos is in Europe" — he actually says "in Europe" before appearing to correct himself



Canudos is in the Brazilian state of Bahia in South America, not Europe. The instructor seems to catch himself but it's an odd slip in a lecture about global history.



[22:19] — "The hotbed of innovation was in the Arabian Peninsula — the most Cosmopolitan center in the world"



This is a significant exaggeration. The Arabian Peninsula at this time was certainly a trading crossroads, and Mecca was an important commercial hub — but describing it as "the most crazy, most open and most Cosmopolitan center in the world" in 600 CE ignores Constantinople, Alexandria, Ctesiphon, and Chang'an, all of which were far larger, wealthier, and more diverse urban centers by any measurable standard. The instructor's framing romanticizes Arabia in a way that doesn't hold up to comparison.



[44:41] — "The real conflict was framed as Muhammad wanting monotheism vs Arab polytheism — this was invented to cover up the revolution"



This is pure speculation presented as historical conclusion. The opposition between Muhammad's monotheism and Meccan polytheism is attested in our earliest non-Islamic sources, including Sebeos himself — the very source the instructor cited earlier. The Sebeos passage he quotes literally says Muhammad told the Arabs they had "abandoned their vain cults" and turned to "the Living God." The monotheism-vs-polytheism conflict isn't a later invention to cover up a revolution — it's in the primary sources from the beginning. The instructor's own evidence contradicts his conclusion.



---



Bottom line: The macro-thesis about social grievances and exhausted empires creating the conditions for Islamic expansion is genuinely interesting and has real support in mainstream scholarship. But it's undermined throughout by basic factual errors on names, texts, dates, and sources — and by presenting speculative interpretive theories as settled historical conclusions. A history class deserves more precision than this.



Full transcript fact-checked by Claude (AI) using non-Islamic historical sources, with strict accuracy standards applied throughout.
